When using Serverless, you may experience 429 Too Many Requests or 503 Service Overloaded. To avoid 429s, you need to stay below our adaptive rate limits. To reduce the likelihood of 503s, you can upgrade to Priority tier

Rate limits are per account and per model — there is no single account-wide token pool. Each model has its own TPM limits, and each model’s adaptive limit grows, shrinks, and resets based only on your usage of that model. Using one model does not consume another model’s limit, and hitting a limit on one model does not rate limit your traffic to other models.
There are three metrics we use to rate limit each account, separately for each model: Total Prompt TPM — input tokens per minute (cached + uncached).
Uncached Prompt TPM — uncached input tokens per minute.
Generated TPM — output tokens per minute.

All limits are measured and enforced in tokens per minute (TPM), per model. For example, exhausting your Total Prompt TPM on one model returns 429 s for that model only — your other models keep their own, unaffected Total Prompt TPM limits. Base adaptive rate limit ceilings depend on the model’s total parameter count. Smaller models get higher base ceilings:

Fast, Priority, and US-only variants of a model share the same tier and ceilings as the base model. Ultra-fast (Preview) has lower rate limits than the standard model (see below). Models without a known parameter count use Large ceilings.

If your traffic ramps up too quickly, you will get 429s.
Historical limit samples for each model are in the Serverless dashboard
Adaptive rate limits have an upper and lower bound. A higher account Spending Tier
correlates with higher upper bound rate limits; enterprise accounts get higher upper bounds automatically.

Adaptive rate limiting is also per model: each model’s limit adapts independently, based only on your recent usage of that model. Ramping up one model does not raise another model’s limit, and going idle on one model does not shrink another model’s limit. Your limit for each model starts at a default value and grows in steps as you use it. Each of the three metrics (Total Prompt TPM, Uncached Prompt TPM, and Generated TPM) has its own standard adaptive limit and changes on its own. Heavy usage on one metric does not change the other standard limits. Under Elastic Burst, high usage on one of these metrics can reduce burst capacity on the others.

Elastic Burst can temporarily raise an eligible account’s current limit above its base ceiling when spare capacity is available. It applies to Total Prompt TPM, Uncached Prompt TPM, and Generated TPM. For eligible accounts and models, Elastic Burst applies automatically to the existing Serverless endpoint; no request or client changes are required. That extra capacity is not guaranteed, and it can change independently of the standard schedule below. If your current limit drops, pace traffic agai

Elastic Burst has no separate enablement fee or burst premium. Usage is billed at your applicable Serverless token rates. To opt out, contact your Fireworks account representative. The opt-out is account-wide and applies across all models for Total Prompt TPM, Uncached Prompt TPM, and Generated TPM.
When limits go up, down, or reset
Your recent usage is above 50% of your current limit. Increases happen at most once every 15 minutes.
Up 25%, capped at your base ceiling
Your highest sampled 15-minute usage over the past 3 days stayed below 33% of your current limit, and at least 24 hours have passed since the limit last changed.
Down 20%, never below the lower bound
You send no traffic to the model for more than 72 hours.
Your usage is above 50% of your current limit and spare capacity is available. It moves back toward your base ceiling when burst headroom goes unused or capacity is needed elsewhere
Increases and decreases vary with available capacity, burst won’t affect your base ceiling
A few details: A decrease is skipped if your recent usage would be at least 50% of the lower limit. This keeps the limit from dropping and then immediately climbing back up.
the increase, decrease, and reset thresholds apply to usage above your reservation and to the adaptive portion of your limit. Usage within the reservation does not count toward the thresholds.
Resets do not apply to accounts with a custom limit or a reservation for that model.
Elastic Burst example: if your current limit is 100M TPM, Elastic Burst can raise it once your usage is above 50M TPM and spare capacity is available.

The steps below follow the standard Decrease row. Elastic Burst capacity can leave without waiting for these daily steps. Say your Total Prompt TPM limit is 10,000,000 and your traffic drops to a steady 1,000,000 tokens per minute: Day
No change. Your earlier, heavier traffic is still in the 3 day window.
First decrease, once the heavy traffic ages out of the window.
Last decrease. 1,000,000 is now more than one third of the limit.
If you stop sending traffic completely, you don’t go through these steps. After more than 72 hours with no traffic, the limit resets to the starting default.
Say your current Total Prompt TPM limit is 1,000,000. Send more than 500,000 but less than 1,000,000 prompt tokens per minute. This keeps you above half your limit without hitting 429s.
More than 15 minutes later, your limit rises to 1,250,000.
Raise your traffic to match, staying between 625,000 and 1,250,000.
Repeat until your limit stops rising.

At this pace, you reach your base ceiling in a few hours. If you are using more than half your limit and it has stopped rising after an increase interval, the standard adaptive limit is at the base ceiling for your spending tier. Moving to a higher spending tier, up to Tier 3, raises the base ceiling, and that limit keeps growing in the same 25% steps. Elastic Burst does not follow these steps. shows historical limit samples, not an instantaneous reading. A Serverless response can include the latest known effective limit in these headers when that limit is known. The value can lag a recent change. X-Ratelimit-Limit-Tokens-Prompt for Total Prompt TPM

These headers are not present on every response. Header values are tokens per minute. Elastic Burst can put these three above the published base ceilings. X-Ratelimit-Limit-Tokens-Cache-Adjusted-Prompt is a separate limit and does not include Elastic Burst. See response headers
Am I guaranteed successful responses up to my rate limit?

No. Staying within your rate limits does not guarantee that every request succeeds. When a deployment is busy, your traffic can still be load shed, and those responses are 503 Service Overloaded. To decrease the chance of being load shed, you can use Priority tier
which is prioritized during high load.

Rate limits — including adaptive rate limiting — are scoped per account and per model. Each model has its own TPM limits and its own adaptive limit, which grows, shrinks, and resets based only on your usage of that model. Traffic to one model does not consume, raise, or lower another model’s limits. Fast and regular model variants have separate limits. Priority tier and regular requests share the same rate limits for a given model.
How is my model's ceiling tier determined?
Ceiling tiers are based on the model’s total parameter count: Small (< 800B), Medium (800B – < 1.6T), or Large (≥ 1.6T). See Model size tiers
for the ceiling values and Models by tier
for where each Serverless model falls.
What should I do first when I see 429s?
Honor the response’s Retry-After header. If it is absent, retry with exponential backoff and jitter.
